manuscript_title: Spaced Review Practice and Grade 8 Algebra Achievement

manuscript_sections.name: abstract
manuscript_sections.text: Background: Algebra achievement in lower secondary school remains low in many public schools. Objective: This study tested whether a spaced-repetition mobile app improves Grade 8 algebra achievement. Methods: A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was used with 96 Grade 8 students (48 treatment, 48 control) from two public schools over eight weeks. Results: The treatment group improved from a mean of 62.4 to 71.8, while the control group improved from 63.1 to 65.2. The difference in gains was statistically significant, t(94) = 4.12, p < .001, d = 0.84. Conclusion: Within this sample, app-based spaced repetition was associated with larger algebra gains than standard practice. Generalization is limited by the non-random assignment.

manuscript_sections.name: introduction
manuscript_sections.text:
Algebra is a gateway subject for later study in mathematics and science, yet many Grade 8 learners in public schools perform below the expected proficiency level. Teachers often report that students forget procedures taught earlier in the term, which limits their ability to build on prior knowledge.
The spacing effect, first described by Ebbinghaus (1885), shows that memory is stronger when practice is distributed over time rather than massed. A later synthesis by Cepeda et al. (2006) confirmed this benefit across many studies. Related work on retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) suggests that testing oneself strengthens retention more than rereading.
Mobile apps can schedule review automatically, but evidence of their effect on algebra achievement in public school settings is limited. This study addresses that gap. The research question was: Does eight weeks of use of a spaced-repetition app improve Grade 8 algebra achievement compared with standard homework practice? The hypothesis was that the treatment group would show larger pretest-to-posttest gains than the control group.

manuscript_sections.name: review of related literature
manuscript_sections.text:
Research on distributed practice shows reliable gains in recall, particularly when the gap between sessions matches the desired retention interval (Cepeda et al., 2006). Retrieval practice adds to this benefit because each review attempt is also a memory test (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
Social learning theory (Bandura, 1977) emphasizes that learners benefit from feedback and from observing successful strategies. Vygotsky (1978) argued that tasks pitched just beyond current ability, with support, promote development. Spaced-repetition apps with adaptive difficulty and immediate feedback can operationalize both ideas.
Taken together, the literature suggests that a scheduled, feedback-rich review tool should improve retention of algebraic procedures. This study tests that prediction in a classroom setting.

manuscript_sections.name: methodology
manuscript_sections.text:
Design. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was used. Two public schools participated; one class per school served as treatment and control respectively.
Participants. A total of 96 Grade 8 students took part, 48 in each group. Mean age was 13.6 years (SD = 0.5). Sample size was based on a power analysis (Cohen, 1988) targeting d = 0.6 at power .80, which required at least 90 participants.
Instrument. A 50-item researcher-made algebra test covering linear equations and expressions was administered before and after the intervention. Content validity was reviewed by three Grade 8 mathematics teachers, and internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha = .84).
Procedure. The treatment group used the app for 15 minutes on four school days each week for eight weeks. The control group completed standard homework of equal time. Informed consent was obtained from parents, and student assent was obtained. The study was approved by the university ethics board before data collection.
Analysis. Gain scores were compared using an independent-samples t-test with alpha = .05, and effect size was reported as Cohen's d.

manuscript_sections.name: results
manuscript_sections.text: The mean gain was 9.4 points for the treatment group and 2.1 points for the control group. This difference in gains was statistically significant, t(94) = 4.12, p < .001, with a large effect size (d = 0.84). No participant dropped out during the eight weeks.

manuscript_sections.name: discussion
manuscript_sections.text:
The results support the hypothesis: students who used the spaced-repetition app improved more than students who completed standard homework. This agrees with the distributed-practice and retrieval-practice literature (Cepeda et al., 2006; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
The effect was larger than the d = 0.6 used in planning. Possible reasons include novelty of the app and the immediate feedback it gave, which fits the support-and-feedback arguments of Bandura (1977) and Vygotsky (1978).
Because assignment to groups was by class and not random, pre-existing class differences may explain part of the result. Teachers' effects were also not controlled.

manuscript_sections.name: limitations and recommendations
manuscript_sections.text:
Limitations include non-random assignment, only two schools, a short eight-week window, and a researcher-made test. Results should not be generalized beyond similar public school settings.
Future studies should use random assignment across more schools, include a delayed posttest to measure retention, and compare spaced-repetition with other forms of digital practice.

manuscript_sections.name: conclusion
manuscript_sections.text:
Within this sample of 96 Grade 8 students, eight weeks of spaced-repetition app use was associated with significantly larger algebra gains than standard homework practice (d = 0.84). Schools may consider piloting such tools, while researchers should replicate the finding with randomized designs.
References
Bandura, A. (1977). Social learning theory. Prentice Hall.
Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.
Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.
Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Duncker & Humblot.
Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society. Harvard University Press.
